I've tilled this ground in Quzhou County for forty years, and the schooling I got means I read the leaf, not just the almanac. My 200 mu feeds four mouths, and that well is the heart of the place.

Right now, my 100 mu of winter wheat is waking up. She got her phosphorus and potassium last autumn, but come regreening I'll top-dress urea in two splits—once at green-up and again at jointing. The well will run four times before the June harvest; a dry spring on the North China Plain can steal half your grain if you let it. One herbicide pass early, and I'll watch for powdery mildew and aphids—if they show, one spray at heading covers me.

June tenth or thereabouts, the wheat comes off and hybrid maize goes in the same afternoon. I don't turn the soil—no-tillage planting right into the stubble. Opening the ground in June just burns off moisture, and these modern hybrids don't need a seedbed fussed over. Two irrigations through summer, herbicide at planting, and one insecticide for corn borer. That same 100 mu gives me two crops in one year, which is how this farm stays profitable.

The remaining 100 mu I split: 40 mu of improved millet and 60 mu of squash. Millet gets rotary tillage in late April, modest fertilizer, and two drinks from the well. It's drought-hardy and the market price for millet never lets me down.

Squash is the crop that defines this farm. I plough deep—those vines want to run—and I load the potassium because fruiting plants are greedy for it. Hybrid seed gives me the vigor and disease resistance I need. Four irrigations, three careful sprays for downy mildew and fruit worms, and I expect a heavy harvest. Done right, that 60 mu of squash pays better than grain.

Every decision is about balancing what the crop needs against what my well and my family can deliver.
